heading: The whole domain in one picture
body: Let us go back over Domain 5 as a whole, before we look at the details. This domain follows one person through one chain of events. First, we find out who is asking. Then we make them prove it. Then we decide what they may do. Then we record what they did. And over time, we keep that access correct as they join, move and leave. Physical and logical controls both play a part, and they cover six assets: information, systems, devices, facilities, applications and services. When a question seems confusing, ask yourself which link in that chain it is really about. Most wrong answers solve a problem from a different link. A stronger password will not help if the real fault is that a person moved jobs and kept the old rights. Find the link, and the answer usually becomes clear.

heading: Factors, and counting them correctly
body: Now let us review the authentication factors, because this is tested again and again. Type 1 is something you know. Type 2 is something you have. Type 3 is something you are or do. Multi-factor authentication means two or more different types. So when you see a scenario, count the types and not the items. A password and a PIN are both known, so that is one factor. Two biometric scans are one factor as well. A smart card and a PIN are two. People mix this up because two steps feel like two factors, and they are not. Remember too that identification is only a claim, and authentication is the proof. When you must choose the best login method, prefer different types of factor, and prefer something that cannot be phished, such as a passkey, over a text message code.

heading: Biometric errors
body: Next come the biometric error rates. Say these aloud until they are automatic. The false rejection rate, or FRR, is a Type 1 error, and it refuses the right person. The false acceptance rate, or FAR, is a Type 2 error, and it lets the wrong person in. The crossover error rate, or CER, is the point where those two are equal. Raising the sensitivity makes FRR go up and FAR go down. To compare two products, use the CER, and remember that lower is better. People go wrong in two ways. They mix up which type is which, or they choose the product with the best single rate, which any vendor can achieve by changing the setting. For a very sensitive door, you may deliberately accept more false rejections to reduce false acceptances. FAR is the error that lets an impostor in.

heading: Sessions, single sign-on and just-in-time
body: Let us now go back over what happens after login. Each person needs one account, because shared accounts destroy accountability. Sessions must end properly. Make tokens random, send them only over encrypted connections, issue a new token at login to stop session fixation, and destroy the session on the server at logout. Ask for fresh proof before risky actions. Single sign-on means fewer passwords and one place to disable a user, but one stolen login opens everything, and an outage stops everything. So pair it with multi-factor authentication, and build it to stay available. Just-in-time access replaces standing privilege with short, approved, logged access that ends by itself. Watch for the second meaning, just-in-time provisioning, which creates an account the first time someone signs in through federation. The exam may use either, so read the scenario closely.

heading: SAML, OAuth and OpenID Connect
body: Now we come to federation, where three names cause endless confusion. The identity provider checks who you are, and the service provider relies on that. SAML is the Security Assertion Markup Language. It uses signed XML assertions, passed through the browser, and is common for business web logins. OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization. It gives an application a limited access token, without giving it your password, and it does not prove who you are. OpenID Connect adds authentication on top of OAuth 2.0, using an ID token in the form of a signed JSON Web Token, and is common for web and mobile logins. So ask what the scenario needs. Permission to reach data means OAuth. Knowing who the person is means OpenID Connect. Signed XML with a business partner means SAML. If a signing key is stolen, replace the key and update trust first, because password resets will not help.

heading: Choosing the authorization model
body: Let us review the authorization models, and one question will separate them all. Who or what decides? In discretionary access control, the owner decides. In mandatory access control, the system compares labels and clearances, and users cannot change them. In role-based control, the person's job decides. In rule-based control, global rules decide for everyone, as on a firewall. In attribute-based control, a combination of facts decides, about the subject, the object, the action and the environment. In risk-based control, the calculated danger of this request decides. Non-discretionary means simply that the owner does not decide, so only discretionary control falls outside it. The common trap is that role-based and rule-based share the same letters, so read the scenario for jobs or for rules. Remember also that clearance alone is never enough. Need to know must also be met.

heading: Matrix, decision and enforcement
body: Two more ideas are short, and easy marks if you keep them straight. In an access control matrix, subjects are the rows and objects are the columns. A row gives you a capability list, which is everything one subject can reach. A column gives you an access control list, which is everyone who can reach one object. So capabilities go with subjects, and access control lists go with objects. Next, the policy decision point evaluates the policy and decides. The policy enforcement point sits in front of the resource and carries out that decision. The picture to hold on to is the manager and the door staff. A gateway in front of an application is usually the enforcement point, even though the request reaches it first. And if the decision point cannot be reached, a sensitive system should deny the request and not simply let it pass.

heading: The access lifecycle
body: Now let us go back over the lifecycle, which is where the manager's mindset shows most clearly. Joiners, movers and leavers should be driven by human resources events. Disable first and delete later, so that records survive. In a hostile termination, disable access at or before the moment the person is told. On a transfer, remove the old rights as the new ones arrive, or privilege creep builds up. Owners and managers review access, and people never review their own. Look for orphan and dormant accounts. Every service account needs a named human owner, least privilege, no interactive login and managed secrets. Sudo should be limited to the commands needed, and its logs should go to a central place that administrators cannot alter. When the same audit finding keeps coming back, the best answer fixes the process. Removing one person's rights only treats the symptom.

heading: Kerberos in order
body: Let us walk through Kerberos one more time, in order. The key distribution center, or KDC, contains the authentication service and the ticket-granting service. The client proves itself to the authentication service and receives a ticket-granting ticket, along with a session key. The client then presents that ticket and an authenticator to the ticket-granting service, and receives a service ticket. Finally, the client presents the service ticket and a new authenticator to the service itself. The password is never sent across the network. Three facts are tested most often. Clocks must match, within five minutes by default. The KDC is a single point of failure and a very valuable target. And Kerberos proves identity, while the service still decides what you may do. It runs on port 88. If forged tickets were made with the KDC's own key, password resets will not help.

heading: RADIUS, TACACS Plus and LDAP
body: Now for the exact facts on network authentication. RADIUS runs over UDP, on port 1812 for authentication and port 1813 for accounting. It protects only the password, and it combines authentication and authorization. It is typically used for Wi-Fi and remote access. TACACS Plus runs over TCP, on port 49. It encrypts the whole message body, and it keeps authentication, authorization and accounting separate, so it can control each command. It is typically used for administrators on routers and switches. The trap is to remember the right facts for the wrong product, so link them together. RADIUS, UDP, password only. TACACS Plus, TCP, whole body. LDAP reads and updates a directory. Port 389 is plain and port 636 is protected with TLS. A simple bind on a plain connection sends the password in clear text, so encrypt it.

heading: Password attacks and thinking like a manager
body: To close, let us match attacks with their defenses, and then remember how to choose the best answer. Spraying is one password against many accounts. Stuffing is reusing leaked logins. Multi-factor authentication stops most of both. Rainbow tables are defeated by salts, and offline cracking is slowed by deliberately slow salted hashes. Lockouts do nothing against an attacker working on a stolen copy. Now the mindset. People's safety comes first, so an escape door fails safe. The asset owner decides who has access, and technical staff carry it out. Prefer the answer that fixes the cause over the one that cleans up a single case. Prefer a control that fits the actual weakness, rather than one that simply sounds strong. Follow the policy in the scenario, and ask which link in the identity chain is really broken. Then choose calmly, like an adviser.
